title: Tasks, channels and bounded asynchronous pipelines
outcome: Build a bounded producer-consumer pipeline, join its work and explain how asynchronous scheduling differs from simultaneous CPU execution.
key_terms: A lightweight unit of concurrent work that runs until it finishes or waits, then lets other tasks proceed.
A typed queue between tasks with a capacity, where `put!` adds an item and `take!` removes one.
A full channel makes `put!` wait until a consumer takes an item, so a fast producer cannot queue unlimited records.
Closing a channel tells consumers that no more values will arrive, so iteration ends after the buffered values are consumed.
The `@sync` block waits for its tasks and throws a `CompositeException` when any of them fails, so errors are not lost.
approach: `squared_pipeline` connects one producer task and one consumer task through `Channel{Int}(2)` inside `@sync`. The producer closes the channel in `finally`, so the consumer's loop always ends, and `@sync` waits for both tasks and rethrows any failure as `CompositeException`. Tasks interleave on one thread here; they do not run simultaneously.

exercises.title: Trace the queue
exercises.task: Describe what happens when a producer fills a capacity-two buffer.
exercises.expected: The next put! waits until space is available.
exercises.answer: The consumer drains a value, allowing the producer to continue without unbounded queue growth.
exercises.why: With capacity 2, a third `put!` blocks until the consumer takes a value, so at most two values wait in the channel.
exercises.wrong: Using an unbounded channel removes the wait but lets a fast producer fill memory when the consumer is slow.
exercises.verify: Print a message before each `put!` and `take!` in an owned copy and observe that puts never run more than two ahead.

exercises.title: Preserve output meaning
exercises.hint: One producer preserves this input order.
exercises.answer: Squares are emitted into the result in channel-consumption order; broader parallel pipelines need explicit ordering.
exercises.why: A single producer puts -2, 0 and 3 in order and the single consumer appends their squares in the same order, giving `[4, 0, 9]`.
exercises.wrong: Assuming the same order holds with several consumers ignores that each can take values at different times.

exercises.title: Inject a failure
exercises.hint: The finally block still closes the channel.
exercises.answer: No shortened result is mislabeled success; joining propagates the producer failure.
exercises.why: `fail_after = 0` makes the producer raise on index 1 before any `put!`; `finally` closes the channel and `@sync` reports `CompositeException`.
exercises.wrong: Wrapping the producer in `try` and swallowing the error returns an empty list that looks like a successful run.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `@test_throws CompositeException squared_pipeline([1]; fail_after = 0)`.

exercises.title: Drain a closed channel
exercises.task: Put 7 into a channel, close it, then collect it.
exercises.expected: The buffered value is still returned.
exercises.hint: Closure means no future puts, not immediate deletion.
exercises.answer: Buffered values can be drained before iteration terminates.
exercises.why: Closing a channel stops future `put!` calls, but the buffered 7 can still be read, so `collect` returns `[7]`.
exercises.wrong: Expecting `close` to discard buffered values loses the last items a producer sent before finishing.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `collect(channel) == [7]`, `!isopen(channel)` and an `InvalidStateException` on a later `put!`.

exercises.title: Identify an unsupported generalization
exercises.task: Explain what can go wrong if an arbitrary consumer callback throws.
exercises.expected: A producer can remain blocked without coordinated cancellation.
exercises.hint: Inspect who closes and who waits.
exercises.answer: The bounded example proves its stated simple consumer path; a generic pipeline needs both failure directions designed.
exercises.why: If the consumer throws, nothing takes from the channel, so a producer blocked on a full buffer waits forever and `@sync` never returns.
exercises.wrong: Assuming the `finally` in the producer handles every failure ignores that it only runs when the producer itself finishes.
exercises.verify: Inject a consumer error in an owned copy with a timeout and design who closes the channel in that direction.

exercises.title: Transfer to file processing
exercises.task: Specify identifiers and completion evidence for concurrent files.
exercises.expected: Use stable file IDs and explicit per-file outcomes.
exercises.hint: A printed line is not a durable acknowledgment.
exercises.answer: Define ordering, retries and partial failure semantics before introducing concurrency.
exercises.why: For files, each result should carry a stable file id and an explicit success or failure outcome so retries and partial runs can be audited.
exercises.wrong: Treating a printed `done` line as completion loses the record if the process stops before output is flushed.
exercises.verify: Write one outcome row per file id and check that the count of rows equals the count of input files.

checks_note: `[2, 2]` and `[4]` add repeated and single-value cases. The `@async 6 * 7` lines show that `fetch` waits for the task and returns 42, after which `istaskdone(job)` is true, which is the same join that `@sync` performs for the pipeline.
